claims.sentence: An electrocardiogram, or ECG, records the electrical activity of the heart.
claims.evidence: BHF/NHS: ECG records the heart's electrical activity; used to check heart rate and rhythm.

claims.sentence: The British Heart Foundation describes it as a simple test that records the heart's rhythm, its rate and its electrical activity.
claims.evidence: BHF: records heart rate/rhythm and electrical activity.

claims.sentence: Each heartbeat is triggered by an electrical signal, and the machine picks these signals up through sensors on the skin.
claims.evidence: Heartbeat is triggered by an electrical signal; NHS says electrodes on skin record the electrical impulses.

claims.sentence: The result is a graph of the signals.
claims.evidence: An ECG trace is a graph of signals; basic fact, not directly retrieved.

claims.sentence: Sticky patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest and connected to the machine.
claims.evidence: NHS: sticky electrodes on arms, legs and chest, wires to the machine.

claims.sentence: A standard 12-lead test uses about ten electrodes to produce twelve views of the heart's signals.
claims.evidence: Search found no source for ten electrodes/twelve views.

claims.sentence: NHS 111 Wales describes the test as usually quick and painless.
claims.evidence: BHF: test takes a few minutes and is completely painless; NHS 111 Wales wording not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The British Heart Foundation describes the test as quick and painless.

claims.sentence: A Whittington Health page says it takes about ten minutes and is not uncomfortable.
claims.evidence: Whittington page not retrieved; NHS page puts the test at about 5 minutes.
claims.newSentence: The NHS puts a standard ECG at about 5 minutes.

claims.sentence: A trust leaflet says the skin may be lightly abraded or shaved so the patches stick, and that creams or oils should not be used on the day.
claims.evidence: Skin abrasion/shaving and creams not found.

claims.sentence: The same leaflet stresses staying relaxed and still, because muscle movement can disturb the recording.
claims.evidence: NHS: you lie still because moving can affect the results.
claims.newSentence: People are asked to lie still because movement can affect the recording.

claims.sentence: Trust pages differ on preparation: one says none is needed, and another says people can eat and drink as normal.
claims.evidence: Not found.

claims.sentence: The British Heart Foundation says an ECG can help doctors to tell whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one in the past.
claims.evidence: BHF: can help doctors tell if you are having a heart attack or have had one in the past.

claims.sentence: Trust factsheets list abnormal heart rhythms, called arrhythmias, coronary heart disease, heart attacks and cardiomyopathy, a disease of the heart muscle, among the conditions it can help to diagnose or monitor.
claims.evidence: NHS: usually done if a doctor thinks you may have symptoms of a heart attack, coronary heart disease or an arrhythmia. Cardiomyopathy not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says an ECG is usually done when a doctor suspects symptoms of a heart attack, coronary heart disease or an abnormal heart rhythm (arrhythmia).

claims.sentence: The tracing can also show features that suggest a person may be at risk of an abnormal rhythm, according to the BHF.
claims.evidence: Not found.

claims.sentence: A standard ECG captures only what happens while it is recording.
claims.evidence: NCBI paper: a 12-lead ECG is a short snapshot and can miss paroxysmal arrhythmias. BHF page not confirmed verbatim.

claims.sentence: It can show an abnormal rhythm only if the rhythm is happening at that time.
claims.evidence: Source says a snapshot can miss paroxysmal arrhythmias; "only if" is stronger.
claims.newSentence: A standard ECG can miss an abnormal rhythm that is not happening during the recording.

claims.sentence: A Sussex factsheet notes that the test has limitations, so further tests may be needed to confirm a diagnosis.
claims.evidence: Not found.

claims.sentence: That is why longer recordings or other heart tests are sometimes arranged.
claims.evidence: Holter/ambulatory monitoring is used to detect arrhythmias a 12-lead snapshot misses.

claims.sentence: An ambulatory ECG, sometimes called Holter monitoring, records the heart's electrical activity continuously while the person goes about daily life.
claims.evidence: NHS: portable recorder worn; Leeds: worn all day and night; PMC: Holters are wearable portable ECGs.

claims.sentence: The BHF says it records for 24 to 48 hours, sometimes longer.
claims.evidence: NHS: usually 24 to 48 hours but can be up to 7 days. Attribution to BHF not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says people are usually asked to wear it for 24 to 48 hours, but it can be up to 7 days.

claims.sentence: It is used for symptoms that come and go, such as palpitations, and it can help to diagnose conditions such as atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm.
claims.evidence: Palpitations and atrial fibrillation not retrieved; general purpose of catching missed rhythms is supported.
claims.newSentence: It is used to look for heart rhythm problems that a short recording may miss.

claims.sentence: One NHS summary says the length of wear is decided by the consultant or GP and can be between 24 hours and seven days.
claims.evidence: Leeds lists 24, 48, 72 hours or 7 days; who decides not retrieved. Covered by revised c20.

claims.sentence: An exercise ECG monitors the heart while the person exercises and the heart is working harder.
claims.evidence: NHS: ECG may be done during exercise; BHF: exercise ECG records heart while walking on treadmill or cycling.

claims.sentence: The BHF describes it as an ECG recorded while the person walks on a treadmill or cycles, and says it shows whether the heart muscle is getting enough blood through the coronary arteries during activity.
claims.evidence: BHF: walk or cycle, used to see how the heart behaves under exertion and look for coronary heart disease. Wording about blood through coronary arteries not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: The British Heart Foundation describes an exercise ECG as an ECG recorded while the person walks on a treadmill or cycles, used to see how the heart behaves under exertion and to look for coronary heart disease.

claims.sentence: Doctors often use it to look into symptoms such as chest pain, palpitations, dizziness and breathlessness.
claims.evidence: BHF mentions dizzy spells or blackouts; chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Doctors may suggest it for symptoms such as dizzy spells or blackouts.

claims.sentence: It is also used after procedures such as angioplasty, and to help set exercise levels for cardiac rehabilitation.
claims.evidence: BHF: may be asked after a procedure such as angioplasty; guides exercise levels in cardiac rehabilitation.

claims.sentence: The person walks or cycles at a gentle pace that gets harder over time, and can stop at any point if they feel unwell.
claims.evidence: BHF: gentle pace, gradually harder, staff watch closely and tell you when to stop. Stopping at any point not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The person walks or cycles at a gentle pace that gradually gets harder, and staff watch closely.

claims.sentence: The report goes to the doctor who requested the ECG.
claims.evidence: Referring doctor receiving report not retrieved for ECG; NHS says a follow-up appointment may be needed.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says people may need a follow-up appointment to talk about their ECG results.

claims.sentence: That doctor then contacts the person to discuss the result.
claims.evidence: Not found.

claims.sentence: For the exercise test, the BHF says the results are sent to the person's doctor, and that the wait can range from a few days to a few weeks.
claims.evidence: NHS: results may be same day but can take a few weeks depending on ECG type. BHF exercise-ECG wait not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says ECG results may be available on the same day, but can take a few weeks depending on the type of ECG.

claims.sentence: Anyone with chest pain that is severe, spreading or accompanied by breathlessness should call 999 and not wait for a test appointment.
claims.evidence: Safety instruction with qualifiers (severe, spreading, breathlessness) not matching source. BHF: call 999 for signs of a heart attack, e.g. sudden chest pain that does not ease after a few minutes of rest.
claims.newSentence: The British Heart Foundation says to call 999 immediately for signs of a heart attack, such as sudden chest pain that does not ease after a few minutes of rest.

claims.sentence: An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart, including its rate and rhythm.
claims.evidence: BHF/NHS: records electrical activity, used to check heart rate and rhythm.

claims.sentence: A standard ECG is quick and painless, and patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest.
claims.evidence: BHF: quick, painless; NHS: electrodes on arms, legs and chest.

claims.sentence: A standard tracing can show an abnormal rhythm only if it is happening during the recording, which is why longer monitoring is sometimes used.
claims.evidence: Snapshot can miss paroxysmal arrhythmias; "only if" too strong.
claims.newSentence: A standard ECG can miss an abnormal rhythm that is not happening during the recording, which is why longer monitoring is sometimes used.

claims.sentence: An ECG can help to show whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one, but other tests may be needed to confirm a diagnosis.
claims.evidence: Heart attack supported; "other tests may be needed" not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: An ECG can help doctors tell whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one in the past.

claims.sentence: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity through patches on the skin. This guide covers the test, longer recordings, what it shows and its limits.
claims.evidence: Records electrical activity via electrodes on skin supported; guide-contents description.

notes: Retrieval was thin (search summaries, few verbatim page texts); strict classification applied.
